A Personal Quick Peek

Meditation

This is my secret to a happy way of life. I practise Vipassana as taught by the late Shri S.N. Goenka in a long tradition of teachers coming from Myanmar, erstwhile Burma. The technique is genuinely pragmatic: focusing on one’s own respiration to calm the mind, leading to a stage where observation of bodily sensations becomes second nature. The key to success, as in any discipline, is perseverance. Over the years I have experienced profound transformation through dedicated practice, which has proved immensely helpful in every walk of life. I can certainly recommend such silent retreats to anyone sincere and on the path of self-discovery. However, I would note that it is not suitable for everyone; the mental disposition of a seeker needs to be in the right frame—that of acceptance. What makes these retreats especially valuable is their non-sectarian, non-dogmatic format, rooted in the Theravada tradition where the Buddha’s actual words have been preserved.

Literature

Poetry is a powerful art—much like an encryption, capable of expressing the core of human emotions in minimal words, making it a science in itself. I find Hindi poetry, especially from the Chhayawaad period (1922–1938), particularly fascinating. This poetic style emphasises a classical approach with Sanskrit vocabulary and strict metrical rules. My favourite poetess is Mahadevi Verma, one of the four pillars of Chhayawaad. A melodious recitation of her work “Jo tum aa jate ek baar” can be found here. My favourite poetic composition is the grand epic Kāmayāni by Jaishankar Prasād, another of the four pillars. Here is a beautiful vocal rendition of a gem from this era called Madhushāla, composed by Harivansh Rai Bachhan, music by Jaidev, and sung by the famous vocalist Manna Dey.

Music

There is something quietly astonishing about the fact that music—one of the most viscerally human experiences, capable of stilling the mind, cracking the heart open, or transporting one to an altogether different dimension of awareness—is at its root an entirely mathematical phenomenon. Vibrations obeying precise frequency ratios, rhythmic cycles governed by arithmetic subdivision, the resonance of harmonic intervals reducible to the simplest fractions: all of it is mathematics, naked and pure. And yet no equation has ever made anyone weep. That paradox, the unbridgeable distance between the formula and the feeling, strikes me as one of the deepest mysteries there is—more inexplicable, in its own way, than quantum entanglement.

This is perhaps why Indian classical music, with its meditative architecture and metaphysical ambitions, resonates so deeply with me. The ancient tradition recognizes sound itself as the primordial substance of the universe—Nāda Brahma, the cosmos as vibration. I am drawn especially to Dhrupad, the oldest surviving form of Hindustani classical music, and in particular to its unhurried opening meditation, the Alaap: a long, wordless, raga-unfolding with no percussion, no hurry, no audience to please—just a human voice feeling its way into the geometry of a scale. Something in that practice mirrors what I find most beautiful about mathematics: the willingness to sit with a structure until it reveals itself. I find the Khayaals and Thumris of the legendary Bade Ghulam Ali Khan inexhaustible in their emotional range, and the Ghazals of Mehdi Hassan almost unbearably tender. The instrumental world of Ravi Shankar’s sitar and Hariprasad Chaurasia’s flute offer a different kind of transport: less about longing, more about a serene, luminous attention that is not unlike the best hours of mathematical work.

Activities

There is a particular quality of presence that only comes from being genuinely tired, in the middle of nowhere, with a mountain still ahead. Long-distance hiking—especially in the Alps, where the scale of things gently dismantles the ego—is one of my deepest pleasures. Something about moving slowly through a vast landscape on one’s own feet, with the mind gradually shedding its noise, produces a clarity of attention that feels akin to meditation, and not entirely unlike the focused stillness that good theoretical physics requires. Cycling shares something of this quality, though with a different rhythm and momentum. I also enjoy cricket, badminton, table tennis, and inline skating whenever time permits, each in its own way a dance between intention and improvisation.

In the realm of stories, I am unashamedly drawn to the epic and the metaphysical. The Lord of the Rings trilogy remains, for me, an unmatched cinematic achievement—not because of its battles, but because of its moral seriousness: the idea that the most important things are done quietly, by people who receive no recognition, in places no song will ever reach. The German series Dark is the other great favourite—a haunting meditation on determinism, free will, and the strange loops of time that, coming from someone who thinks about spacetime for a living, hits rather closer to home than most fiction. The American series Lost completes the triangle: an island, unanswerable questions, and characters whose inner lives matter as much as the mythology surrounding them. What all three share, I think, is a willingness to sit with mystery rather than resolve it cheaply—which, in the end, is also the only honest attitude one can take toward the universe.
